Reading Virgil's version of the same crossing lets them see how an ancient myth and a modern novel build the same place.","enduringUnderstanding":"Authors retell old stories by keeping familiar patterns and changing details, and language choices create the tone and mood that show what each version values.","futureLessons":"In Chapter 19 students will keep studying Riordan's updated afterlife. The comparison skills and abstract-noun topic sentences from today return in later writing and discussion.","performanceTask":"The Shared Stories, Shared Lessons task asks students to compare two depictions of the same setting and analyze tone. Picture the way Percy enters the Underworld in Chapter 18. Which details stand out?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do you remember about how Percy and his friends arrive in the Underworld and who or what they meet?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They go through a place that looks like a modern building, and there are lots of dead people waiting. They have to cross a river, and a boatman is in charge of the crossing."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Riordan did not invent this crossing. Writers have told about it for about two thousand years. Today you will compare his version with Virgil's and write about what Riordan keeps and what he changes."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Teach how abstract nouns anchor a topic sentence, and review pronoun shifts so students can write formally and correctly.","activities":[{"id":"lab-abstract-noun-topic-sentence","title":"Abstract Nouns as Thematic Anchors","minutes":6,"standards":["W.6.2.a","W.6.2.e","L.6.6"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"An abstract noun names an idea you cannot touch, such as authority, destiny, loyalty, justice or apathy. Putting one in your topic sentence tells readers the big idea your paragraph will explain."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Plain: Riordan's underworld is different from Virgil's. Anchored: Riordan keeps the ancient idea of authority over the crossing but changes how that authority looks in a modern world."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What abstract noun anchors the second sentence, and how does it help the reader?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The word is authority. It tells me the paragraph will be about who is in charge of the crossing, so I know what to look for."},{"type":"directions","text":"With a partner, choose one abstract noun from the list (authority, destiny, loyalty, justice, apathy, betrayal) and draft a topic sentence about the two underworld crossings."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Accept any noun that fits. Apathy can describe the bored guard and the crowds of waiting souls. Destiny can describe the fate of the dead."}]},{"id":"lab-pronoun-shifts","title":"Pronoun Shifts Mini-Review","minutes":4,"standards":["L.6.1.c","L.6.1"],"routine":"Quick Edit","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Keep pronouns consistent in number and person. A shift to *you* in formal writing is a common mistake."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Incorrect: When a reader enters Virgil's underworld, you see crowds of souls. Also: Each soul waits for their turn, and you hope to cross."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How can we fix these sentences?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"When a reader enters Virgil's underworld, he or she sees crowds of souls, or better, readers see crowds of souls. Each soul waits for its turn, or souls wait for their turn."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Everyday speech accepts singular *their*. Focus on the shift from third person to *you*. Students should write formally with third person."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students gather evidence from both texts, analyze imagery and word choice for tone and mood, and write a comparison paragraph.","activities":[{"id":"lia-evidence-chart","title":"Gather Evidence From Both Texts","minutes":10,"standards":["W.6.9","RL.6.1","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 18","pages":"pp. 291-299"},{"type":"text-reference","title":"Aeneid, Book 6 excerpt","pages":"lines 295-336"},{"type":"directions","text":"Make a three-column chart: Detail, Aeneid, Lightning Thief. Add rows for the crowd of souls, the river, and the ferryman. Record a short quote or paraphrase in each box and note the page or line."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does each text present the crowd of souls, the river and the ferryman?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the Aeneid, huge crowds of souls crowd the bank of a dark river, and the ferryman is a squalid old man. In the novel, the dead wait in a modern place, and the boatman works for the Underworld in a modern way. Both have the crowd, the river and the ferryman."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.9"],"stem":"Which detail appears in BOTH Virgil's excerpt and Chapter 18?","choices":[{"text":"A ferryman figure who controls the crossing of a river","correct":true,"rationale":"Both texts include a boatman at the river that the dead must cross."},{"text":"A modern waiting room with a security guard","correct":false,"rationale":"This modern setting is Riordan's change, not in Virgil."},{"text":"A hero who defeats the ferryman in battle","correct":false,"rationale":"Neither text shows this; students may confuse it with other myths."},{"text":"Souls who are happy to be in the underworld","correct":false,"rationale":"Both texts present the dead as waiting and unhappy, not happy."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students name details precisely and compare two texts orally before writing.","sayAsk":"Say: Point to the detail and say it. In the Aeneid, ___. In Chapter 18, ___. Both texts have ___. You said the water is bad; we can say the water is murky and fathomless.","watchFor":"If students list details from only one text, then prompt: What is the matching detail in the other text? Success: student pairs a detail from each text with page or line evidence."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding details in Virgil's translation","tryThis":"Give line ranges for the crowd, the river and the ferryman, and have students underline them before charting."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to add a row for the setting's rules and explain what each text suggests about who has authority."}]}]},{"id":"lia-tone-mood","title":"Analyze Imagery, Word Choice, Tone and Mood","minutes":8,"standards":["RL.6.4","W.6.2.d"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Choose two words or phrases from each text (for example, fathomless water and squalid ferryman in Virgil; the DOA setting and the boatman in Riordan). Explain how each creates tone and mood."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the word choice in each text create mood?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Virgil's words like fathomless and squalid make the mood gloomy and frightening and the tone solemn. Riordan's modern DOA setting adds humor, so the mood is more playful but still creepy."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support evaluating language choices and adding details with adverbials.","sayAsk":"Say: The word ___ makes the mood feel ___. Expand with adverbials: The souls wait *by the dark river*. The guard answers *slowly and without interest*.","watchFor":"If students say only 'it's scary', then prompt: Which word makes it feel that way? Success: student names a word and its effect."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: naming tone versus mood","tryThis":"Tone is the author's attitude; mood is the reader's feeling. Offer a word bank: gloomy, solemn, humorous, eerie, bored."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students explain how the modern details change what the crossing says about death."}]}]},{"id":"lia-draft-paragraph","title":"Write the Comparison Paragraph","minutes":12,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.4","W.6.2.a","W.6.2.b","W.6.2.c","W.6.2.f","W.6.5","W.6.10"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Model your plan: topic sentence with an abstract noun, one honors detail, one change detail, tone or mood, then a concluding sentence."},{"type":"directions","text":"Write a paragraph comparing Riordan's modern underworld crossing with Virgil's classical version. Explain how the novel both honors and changes the older myth. Include a topic sentence with an abstract noun, at least two details from each text, transitions such as similarly, however and as a result, and a concluding sentence. Use formal third-person style."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Riordan honors the ancient idea of authority over the crossing while changing it for a contemporary world. Like Virgil, he shows crowds of souls waiting by a dark river and a ferryman who controls who crosses. However, Virgil describes fathomless water and a squalid ferryman, which creates a gloomy, solemn mood. In contrast, Riordan's modern DOA setting and boatman add humor, so the mood is eerie but also playful. As a result, readers recognize the old myth in a new setting. Overall, the novel keeps the myth's shape but changes its tone."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support writing a structured comparison with transitions and expanded sentences.","sayAsk":"Say: Like Virgil, Riordan ___. However, in the novel, ___. As a result, ___. Expand: The ferryman waits *silently at the river*.","watchFor":"If students only list differences, then prompt: What does Riordan keep? Success: paragraph shows both honoring and changing, with evidence."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: starting the paragraph","tryThis":"Offer the frame: Riordan honors the idea of ___ but changes ___ by ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Challenge students to add a sentence explaining what the changes suggest about how modern readers think about death, and to replace a simple connector with a more precise transition."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on what they learned about how authors retell myths.","activities":[{"id":"lookback-turn-talk","title":"Honor and Change","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9","W.6.4"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Read your topic sentence aloud to a partner. Tell your partner one thing Riordan honors and one thing he changes."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why might Riordan keep some parts of the old myth and change others?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"He keeps the crossing so readers who know the myth recognize it, but he changes the setting so it feels real and funny to modern readers."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Optional reading to prepare for the next lesson.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-ch19","title":"Read and Annotate Chapter 19","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.10"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 19","pages":"pp. 300-309"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read and annotate Chapter 19. Mark details that show how Riordan updates the afterlife."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students compared Riordan's Chapter 18 underworld crossing with Virgil's Aeneid excerpt, analyzing imagery, tone and mood.
